opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I'll be honest: computing exact Shapley values is not practical at web scale. The exact computation means considering every possible coalition of contributors and measuring each one's marginal contribution, which grows exponentially. With billions of documents feeding into a model or an answer, that's simply impossible.

But I don't think the exact math is the point. The Shapley value is useful as a north star for what fairness should look like: if your content contributed to the value that got created, you should share in that value, in proportion to how much it actually mattered. Then the question becomes how well you can approximate it, and whether the approximation is good enough that people trust it.

The setting matters a lot. For training data, attribution is very hard because a model's capabilities come from diffuse influence across a huge corpus. At inference time, though, when an agent or model retrieves a specific set of pages to answer a specific question, the problem becomes much more tractable. You're dealing with tens of sources, not billions. You can run counterfactuals, like whether the answer changes meaningfully if a particular source is removed, and use sampling-based approximations that converge reasonably well. That's real engineering, not science fiction.

There are practical issues beyond computation. One is gaming: as soon as there's money attached, people will try to create content designed to look influential rather than be useful, so the mechanism has to be robust to that. Another is legibility: content owners need to understand roughly why they got paid what they got paid, or the system won't earn trust even if it's mathematically elegant.

So my view is that exact Shapley values aren't practical, but approximate, Shapley-inspired attribution, especially at the point of retrieval and use, is practical. It's probably one of the more important pieces of infrastructure to get right if we want an open web that keeps getting created in a world where more and more of the consumption is done by AI rather than people clicking on links. If the people creating the content can't get paid, the content stops getting created, and that's bad for everyone, including the AI systems.

r001.rationale: The response says exact Shapley computation is impractical and grows exponentially, but does not compare its cost with running the agent.

r002.rationale: The response mentions sampling-based approximations that converge reasonably well, but does not state that accurate estimates can be produced using appropriately constructed data and models.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing to say is that the exact Shapley value is basically a theoretical object. It's beautiful, it has all the axioms you want, fairness properties, symmetry, the whole thing. But computing it exactly means you'd need to look at every possible subset of your data, retrain or re-evaluate the model on each one, and the number of subsets is exponential in the number of contributors. When your "players" are hundreds of millions of web pages, that's just not a thing anyone is going to do, ever.

So the honest answer is nobody computes Shapley values at web scale. What you can do is approximate them. There's a whole line of work, Monte Carlo sampling of permutations, things like Data Shapley, TracIn, influence functions, where you're trying to get a cheap, noisy estimate of marginal contribution. And those are useful, but you have to be clear-eyed about what you're getting. The estimates are high variance, they're sensitive to how you define the utility function, and the influence of any one page on a model trained on trillions of tokens is going to be vanishingly small and incredibly hard to distinguish from noise. So you end up in a world where the theoretically "right" number for most individual contributors is some tiny fraction that you can't even measure reliably.

The way I think about it is, Shapley values are more useful as a conceptual anchor than as a billing system. They tell you what fairness would look like in principle, and that helps you reason about which simpler proxies are reasonable. In practice, you probably end up with something much coarser: attribution at the level of a source or domain rather than a page, measured at inference time rather than training time, because at inference time you actually know what you retrieved and what you cited. That's tractable. If a model grounds an answer on three sources, you can share value with those three sources. That's not a Shapley value, but it's directionally correct and it's auditable, which matters a lot if you're actually moving money.

And then there's the other practical point, which is that the market will probably care more about simplicity and predictability than about theoretical purity. Content owners want to understand why they got paid what they got paid. A number that comes out of a sampled approximation of an exponential computation is hard to argue with but also hard to trust. So I'd rather have a system that's legible and roughly fair than one that's precisely fair and completely opaque. Use the theory to sanity-check your heuristics, but build the heuristics.

r001.rationale: The response says exact Shapley computation is exponential and impractical at web scale, but does not compare its cost with running the agent itself.

r002.rationale: The response describes estimates as noisy, high variance, and hard to measure reliably; it does not state they can be estimated accurately using appropriately constructed data and models.

astra-6.text:
I think Shapley values give you a useful theoretical framework for thinking about contribution, but computing them exactly at the scale of the web is impractical. You’re asking how much each piece of content adds across all the different combinations of content you could have trained on. You can’t retrain a model for every one of those combinations.

You could approximate that, but then you have to ask what you’re measuring. Is it improvement in some benchmark? Is it usefulness to a particular user? Those choices affect what you conclude a piece of content is worth.

So I’d separate the question of understanding contribution from the question of setting payments. Attribution can inform a payment system, but you still need a practical agreement about what gets rewarded and how.

r002.rationale: The response says Shapley values could be approximated, but does not state they can be estimated accurately using appropriately constructed data and models.

sol-6.1.text:
I think Shapley values are a useful conceptual framework, but making them a practical payment mechanism is much harder. You’re asking how much a particular piece of content contributes across all the different combinations of data you could have trained on. Computing that exactly is prohibitively expensive at this scale.

You can approximate it, but then you have to ask what you’re measuring. Is it improvement in average model performance? Performance on a particular task? And if two websites contain essentially the same information, how should you divide the value between them? Those choices can change the answer substantially.

So I’d distinguish having a principled way to think about contribution from having a system you can actually use to pay people. Shapley values might inform that system, but I wouldn’t assume they give us a uniquely correct or practical price for every piece of content.

r001.rationale: It says exact computation is prohibitively expensive at this scale, but does not compare its cost with running the agent itself.

r002.rationale: It says Shapley values can be approximated, but does not state that accurate estimates are possible using appropriately constructed data and models.
